title: Sum of Divisors Function: Properties and Classification
description: Formalizes the arithmetic function σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d with concrete values, multiplicativity, prime power formula, and number classification. Proves σ(p) = p+1 for all primes, σ(mn) = σ(m)σ(n) when gcd(m,n)=1, σ(p^k) = Σ p^i, and classifies deficient/perfect/abundant numbers. Verifies amicable pairs (220,284) and (1184,1210). Proves 12 is the smallest abundant number. 81 theorems, 4 definitions, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified using Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction.sigma.
originalContributions: IsDeficient / IsPerfect / IsAbundant: classification predicates (new definitions)
six_is_perfect / twenty_eight_is_perfect: first two perfect numbers verified
twelve_abundant / smallest_abundant: 12 is the smallest abundant number (minimality proof)

overview.historicalContext: The sum of divisors function σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d is one of the oldest objects in number theory. Perfect numbers — where σ(n) = 2n, or equivalently n equals the sum of its proper divisors — fascinated ancient Greek mathematicians: Euclid (c. 300 BCE) proved that 2^(p-1)(2^p-1) is perfect whenever 2^p-1 is prime (Mersenne prime). Euler (1747) proved the converse: every even perfect number has this form. Whether odd perfect numbers exist remains one of mathematics' oldest unsolved problems. Amicable pairs were known to the Pythagoreans: (220, 284) appears in the works of Iamblichus (c. 300 CE). Thabit ibn Qurra (9th century) gave a rule for generating amicable pairs; Euler found 58 more. Remarkably, the second-smallest pair (1184, 1210) was discovered by 16-year-old Niccolò Paganini in 1866, having been missed by Euler and others. The Dirichlet series of σ is Σ σ(n)/n^s = ζ(s)ζ(s-1), connecting σ to the Riemann zeta function. Robin's inequality σ(n) < e^γ n ln(ln(n)) for all n > 5040 is equivalent to the Riemann Hypothesis (Robin, 1984). Gronwall's theorem shows lim sup σ(n)/(n ln(ln(n))) = e^γ ≈ 1.78. This file formalizes the algebraic properties of σ — multiplicativity, prime power formula, number classification — that form the computational foundation of all these deeper results.
overview.problemStatement: Formalize σ(n) = Σ_{d|n} d with its key properties: concrete values, multiplicativity, prime power formula, number classification (deficient/perfect/abundant), and amicable pairs.
overview.text: The function σ(n) counts the total 'divisor weight' of n. Key structural result: σ is multiplicative — coprime inputs multiply σ values. For prime powers: σ(p^k) = (p^(k+1)-1)/(p-1). For primes: σ(p) = p+1. This lets σ be computed from the prime factorization. Numbers are classified by σ(n) vs 2n: deficient (σ<2n), perfect (σ=2n), abundant (σ>2n). Amicable pairs (a,b) satisfy σ(a)=a+b and σ(b)=a+b.
overview.proofStrategy: Use Mathlib's ArithmeticFunction.sigma and native_decide for concrete computations. Prove general multiplicativity and prime power formula via algebraic manipulations. Derive classification predicates and verify all examples computationally.
keyInsights: Multiplicativity reduces σ computation from any n to prime powers: σ(p₁^a₁·p₂^a₂·...) = σ(p₁^a₁)·σ(p₂^a₂)·... — this is why Mathlib's one-liner `isMultiplicative_sigma.map_mul_of_coprime` is the algebraic core
σ(p^k) = 1+p+...+p^k = (p^(k+1)-1)/(p-1) is a geometric sum — the key building block; combined with multiplicativity, gives a closed-form formula for σ(n) from prime factorization
Classification by omega: `IsDeficient ∨ IsPerfect ∨ IsAbundant` and all exclusivity theorems reduce to trichotomy of σ(n) vs 2n, closed entirely by the `omega` tactic
Amicable pairs encode a symmetric relation: (m,n) amicable ↔ σ(m)=σ(n)=m+n; the Pythagorean pair (220,284) and Paganini's pair (1184,1210) are both machine-verified
Minimality via interval_cases: proving 12 is the smallest abundant number uses Lean's `interval_cases` to case-split over all n∈{1,...,11}, verifying each by native_decide
Robin's inequality connects σ to the Riemann Hypothesis: σ(n) < e^γ n ln(ln(n)) for all n > 5040 iff RH holds — the properties formalized here are the starting point for this deep connection
prerequisites: Arithmetic functions: multiplicative functions, Dirichlet convolution
Number classification: perfect, deficient, abundant numbers

conclusion.summary: Sum of divisors function fully formalized: concrete values, multiplicativity, prime power formula, complete number classification (deficient/perfect/abundant with exhaustivity and exclusivity), amicable pairs (220,284) and (1184,1210), 12 as smallest abundant. 81 theorems, 549 lines, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: This formalization provides the algebraic infrastructure for one of number theory's richest subjects. The multiplicativity of σ connects via Dirichlet series to ζ(s)ζ(s-1), linking divisor sums to the Riemann zeta function. Robin's theorem (1984) shows σ(n) < e^γ n ln(ln(n)) for n > 5040 iff RH holds — a startling connection between a simple arithmetic function and the most famous open problem in mathematics. The classification into deficient/perfect/abundant has been studied since Nicomachus (~100 CE), yet the question of odd perfect numbers remains unsolved after 2000 years of effort.
openQuestions: Are there odd perfect numbers? This 2000-year-old problem remains unsolved; any odd perfect number must be > 10^1500 and have at least 101 prime factors
Are there infinitely many perfect numbers? Equivalent to asking whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes (open)
Formalize Euler's theorem: every even perfect number has the form 2^(p-1)(2^p-1) where 2^p-1 is prime — this would complete the classification of even perfect numbers
Formalize Robin's inequality: prove σ(n) < e^γ n ln(ln(n)) for small n and connect it to the Riemann Hypothesis formalization

sections.title: Module Header and Status
sections.summary: Documents the 14-part structure covering σ values, primes, classification, amicable pairs, abundancy, divisor count, σ₂, bounds, connections to RH, multiplicativity, prime power formula, factorization computation, and minimality. Imports Mathlib and opens SumOfDivisors namespace.
sections.mathContext: The sum-of-divisors function $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$ is one of the central objects in multiplicative number theory. It generalizes to $\sigma_k(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d^k$, with $\sigma_0(n)$ counting divisors and $\sigma_1(n) = \sigma(n)$ summing them. Mathlib formalizes this as $\mathtt{ArithmeticFunction.sigma}\, k\, n$. This module builds a comprehensive Lean 4 library around $\sigma$: concrete evaluations, algebraic structure (multiplicativity), classification theory, and connections to deep open problems like the odd perfect number question and Robin's inequality linking $\sigma$ to the Riemann Hypothesis.

sections.title: Part 1: Concrete σ Values
sections.summary: Verifies σ(1) through σ(10), σ(12), σ(28), σ(100) using native_decide. Establishes the empirical foundation: σ(6)=12, σ(28)=56 (perfect numbers), σ(12)=28 (abundant).
sections.mathContext: Concrete values anchor the theory: $\sigma(1) = 1$ (only divisor is $1$), $\sigma(p) = p+1$ for primes (divisors $\{1, p\}$), $\sigma(4) = 1+2+4 = 7$, $\sigma(6) = 1+2+3+6 = 12$, and $\sigma(28) = 1+2+4+7+14+28 = 56$. The equalities $\sigma(6) = 2 \cdot 6$ and $\sigma(28) = 2 \cdot 28$ witness that $6$ and $28$ are perfect numbers. Similarly $\sigma(12) = 1+2+3+4+6+12 = 28 > 24 = 2 \cdot 12$ witnesses abundance. These values are verified by $\mathtt{native\_decide}$, which reduces the goal to a decision procedure evaluated at compile time.

sections.title: Parts 2: σ on Primes
sections.summary: Verifies σ(p) = p+1 for p = 2,3,5,7,11,13 by native_decide, then proves the general theorem for all primes using sigma_apply_prime_pow + simp + linarith.
sections.mathContext: For a prime $p$, the divisors of $p$ are exactly $\{1, p\}$, so $\sigma(p) = 1 + p = p + 1$. This is a special case of the prime power formula: $\sigma(p^1) = \sum_{i=0}^{1} p^i = 1 + p$. The general proof uses Mathlib's $\mathtt{sigma\_apply\_prime\_pow}$, which gives $\sigma(p^k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} p^i$ for any prime $p$ and $k \geq 0$. At $k=1$ this simplifies to $1 + p^1 = p + 1$ via $\mathtt{simp}$ and $\mathtt{linarith}$. This theorem is used throughout the classification section since all primes are deficient: $\sigma(p) = p + 1 < 2p$ for $p \geq 2$.

sections.title: Part 3: Number Classification (Deficient/Perfect/Abundant)
sections.summary: Defines IsDeficient, IsPerfect, IsAbundant predicates. Proves primes and powers of 2 are deficient; 6, 28, 496 are perfect; 12, 18, 20, 24 are abundant. Uses native_decide for all concrete verifications.
sections.mathContext: The three classification predicates partition the positive integers by comparing $\sigma(n)$ with $2n$: $\mathtt{IsDeficient}(n) \iff \sigma(n) < 2n$, $\mathtt{IsPerfect}(n) \iff \sigma(n) = 2n$, and $\mathtt{IsAbundant}(n) \iff \sigma(n) > 2n$. Equivalently, $n$ is perfect when $n$ equals the sum of its proper divisors. Primes are deficient because $\sigma(p) = p+1 < 2p$. Powers of $2$ are deficient: $\sigma(2^k) = 2^{k+1} - 1 < 2^{k+1}$. The three known perfect numbers in this file are $6 = 2^1(2^2-1)$, $28 = 2^2(2^3-1)$, and $496 = 2^4(2^5-1)$, all of the Euclid–Euler form $2^{p-1}(2^p-1)$ with $2^p-1$ prime.

sections.title: Part 4: Classification Theory (Exhaustive and Exclusive)
sections.summary: Proves classification_exhaustive (every n is one of the three types) and three exclusivity theorems. All proved by omega after unfolding definitions — trichotomy of σ(n) vs 2n.
sections.mathContext:
The classification is a partition: for any $n > 0$, exactly one of $\sigma(n) < 2n$, $\sigma(n) = 2n$, $\sigma(n) > 2n$ holds. This is the trichotomy of the natural numbers (or integers), so after unfolding the definitions, all goals reduce to $\mathtt{omega}$ — the linear arithmetic decision procedure. The exclusivity theorems are: $\mathtt{IsPerfect}(n) 	o 
eg\mathtt{IsDeficient}(n)$, $\mathtt{IsAbundant}(n) 	o 
eg\mathtt{IsPerfect}(n)$, and $\mathtt{IsDeficient}(n) 	o 
eg\mathtt{IsAbundant}(n)$. Together with exhaustivity, these confirm the predicates form a partition of $\mathbb{N}_{>0}$.

sections.title: Part 5: Amicable Numbers
sections.summary: Defines AreAmicable. Verifies σ(220)=504, σ(284)=504 (Pythagorean pair) and σ(1184)=2394, σ(1210)=2394 (Paganini's pair) by native_decide, then proves amicability by omega.
sections.mathContext: Two distinct numbers $m, n$ form an amicable pair if $\sigma(m) = m + n$ and $\sigma(n) = m + n$, i.e., each is the sum of the proper divisors of the other. The condition $\sigma(m) = \sigma(n) = m + n$ is symmetric: $(m, n)$ amicable iff $(n, m)$ amicable. For the Pythagorean pair: $220 = 2^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 11$ and $284 = 2^2 \cdot 71$, with $\sigma(220) = \sigma(284) = 504 = 220 + 284$. For Paganini's pair: $1184 = 2^5 \cdot 37$ and $1210 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 11^2$, with $\sigma(1184) = \sigma(1210) = 2394 = 1184 + 1210$. These are verified numerically by $\mathtt{native\_decide}$ and then the amicability condition is discharged by $\mathtt{omega}$.

sections.title: Part 6: Abundancy Index
sections.summary: Defines abundancy index σ(n)/n as a rational number. Proves perfect ↔ abundancy = 2 (for n > 0) via field_simp + exact_mod_cast + omega.
sections.mathContext: The abundancy index of $n$ is the rational number $I(n) = \sigma(n)/n$. It satisfies $I(n) \geq 1$ for all $n \geq 1$ (since $n \mid n$ contributes $n$ to $\sigma(n)$), with $I(1) = 1$ and $I(p) = (p+1)/p$ for primes. The classification becomes: $n$ is deficient iff $I(n) < 2$, perfect iff $I(n) = 2$, abundant iff $I(n) > 2$. Multiplicativity of $\sigma$ implies that $I(mn) = I(m) \cdot I(n)$ when $\gcd(m,n)=1$. The formal proof that $\mathtt{IsPerfect}(n) \leftrightarrow I(n) = 2$ unfolds as $\sigma(n) = 2n \leftrightarrow \sigma(n)/n = 2$, proved by $\mathtt{field\_simp}$ (clearing the denominator $n > 0$) and $\mathtt{omega}$.

sections.title: Parts 7-8: Divisor Count and σ₂
sections.summary: Computes d(n) = σ_0(n) (divisor count) for n=1,2,4,6,12,1024 and σ_2(n) (sum of squared divisors) for n=1,2,6 by native_decide.
sections.mathContext: The family $\sigma_k(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d^k$ generalizes $\sigma$: $\sigma_0(n) = d(n)$ counts divisors, $\sigma_1(n) = \sigma(n)$ sums them, and $\sigma_2(n)$ sums their squares. All are multiplicative. Representative values: $d(12) = 6$ (divisors $1,2,3,4,6,12$), $d(1024) = d(2^{10}) = 11$. For $\sigma_2$: $\sigma_2(6) = 1^2 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 6^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 + 36 = 50$. The Dirichlet series encode the generating functions: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty d(n)/n^s = \zeta(s)^2$ and $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma(n)/n^s = \zeta(s)\zeta(s-1)$, connecting these functions to the Riemann zeta function.

sections.title: Part 9: Key Bounds
sections.summary: Proves σ(n) ≥ n for n ≥ 1 (using n ∈ divisors) and σ(n) > n for n > 1 (using {1,n} ⊆ divisors, Finset.sum_pair). General proofs use Finset.single_le_sum and sum_le_sum_of_subset.
sections.mathContext: The lower bounds on $\sigma$ reflect the structure of divisors. For $n \geq 1$: since $n \mid n$, we have $n \in \{d : d \mid n\}$, so $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d \geq n$ by $\mathtt{Finset.single\_le\_sum}$. For $n > 1$: both $1$ and $n$ are divisors and $1 \neq n$, so $\sigma(n) \geq 1 + n > n$ using $\mathtt{Finset.sum\_pair}$. Upper bounds are subtler: by Gronwall's theorem, $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sigma(n)/(n \ln \ln n) = e^\gamma \approx 1.7811$, where $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. These bounds are foundational for all classification results since $\sigma(n) \geq n$ implies $I(n) \geq 1$.

sections.title: Part 10: Connections to Robin's Inequality and RH
sections.summary: Documentation section: Robin's inequality (σ(n) < e^γ n ln(ln(n)) for n ≥ 5041 iff RH), Gronwall's theorem (lim sup = e^γ), Ramanujan highly composite numbers. No Lean proofs — theoretical context only.
sections.mathContext: Robin's theorem (1984) gives a remarkable equivalence: the Riemann Hypothesis holds if and only if $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma n \ln(\ln(n))$ for all $n > 5040$, where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant and $e^\gamma \approx 1.7811$. The inequality is known to hold for all $n \leq 5040$ (verified by exhaustion) and for all $n > 5040$ conditionally on RH. Gronwall's theorem (1913) gives the complementary asymptotic: $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sigma(n) / (n \ln \ln n) = e^\gamma$. The extremal cases are Colossally abundant numbers (Ramanujan's highly composite numbers), which saturate the bound. This deep connection places $\sigma$ at the intersection of elementary and analytic number theory.

sections.title: Part 11: Multiplicativity of σ
sections.summary: Proves σ_k is multiplicative (one-line from isMultiplicative_sigma) and the coprime product formula σ(mn) = σ(m)σ(n). Demonstrates with examples: σ(6)=σ(2)σ(3), σ(12)=σ(4)σ(3), σ(30)=σ(2)σ(15).
sections.mathContext: An arithmetic function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is multiplicative if $f(1) = 1$ and $f(mn) = f(m)f(n)$ whenever $\gcd(m,n) = 1$. The function $\sigma$ is multiplicative, which follows from the fact that $\sigma = \mathbf{1} * \mathrm{id}$ (Dirichlet convolution of the constant-$1$ function with the identity), and Dirichlet convolution of multiplicative functions is multiplicative. In Lean, this is $\mathtt{isMultiplicative\_sigma}$. The coprime product formula $\sigma(mn) = \sigma(m)\sigma(n)$ for $\gcd(m,n) = 1$ reduces computation to prime powers: $\sigma(2^2 \cdot 3) = \sigma(4) \cdot \sigma(3) = 7 \cdot 4 = 28$. This is the key reduction that makes $\sigma$ tractable.

sections.title: Parts 12-13: σ on Prime Powers and Factorization
sections.summary: Proves σ(p^k) = Σ_{i=0}^k p^i by sigma_apply_prime_pow. Specializes to k=1,2,3. Demonstrates factorization-based computation: σ(12) = (1+2+4)(1+3) = 28, σ(30) = (1+2)(1+3)(1+5) = 72.
sections.mathContext: The prime power formula is $\sigma(p^k) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} p^i = \frac{p^{k+1}-1}{p-1}$ (a geometric series). This follows because the divisors of $p^k$ are exactly $\{1, p, p^2, \ldots, p^k\}$. Specializations: $\sigma(p^2) = 1 + p + p^2$ and $\sigma(p^3) = 1 + p + p^2 + p^3$. Combined with multiplicativity, this gives a closed-form formula from the prime factorization: if $n = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_r^{a_r}$ then $\sigma(n) = \prod_{i=1}^r \frac{p_i^{a_i+1}-1}{p_i-1}$. For example $\sigma(30) = \sigma(2)\sigma(3)\sigma(5) = 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 72$. In Lean, $\mathtt{sigma\_apply\_prime\_pow}$ provides the Finset sum form used to prove each specialization.

sections.title: Part 14: 12 is the Smallest Abundant Number
sections.summary: Proves not_abundant_lt_12 (∀ 0<n<12, ¬IsAbundant n) by interval_cases + native_decide, then twelve_smallest_abundant combining this with twelve_is_abundant.
sections.mathContext: To prove $12$ is the smallest abundant number, two facts are needed: (1) $12$ is abundant ($\sigma(12) = 28 > 24 = 2 \cdot 12$), and (2) no $n$ with $1 \leq n < 12$ is abundant. The proof of (2) uses $\mathtt{interval\_cases}\, n$, which case-splits the goal into 11 subgoals for $n = 1, 2, \ldots, 11$; each is dispatched by $\mathtt{native\_decide}$ verifying $\sigma(n) \leq 2n$. The combined theorem $\mathtt{twelve\_smallest\_abundant}$ states $\forall m, 0 < m \to \mathtt{IsAbundant}(m) \to m \geq 12$, established by contrapositive: if $m < 12$ then $m$ is not abundant. The density of abundant numbers is approximately $24.76\%$ of all positive integers (Deléglise, 1998).
